Lessons.Title: Representing Sequences
ExplanationParagraphs: Translate among a list, table, graph and recursive definition; calculate common differences and growth factors.

A sequence can be represented as indexed terms, an input-output table, discrete graph points or a recurrence. For 5,15,25,35,45 the common difference is 10. For g(1)=-5 and g(n)=-2g(n-1), the first four terms are -5,10,-20,40. A geometric list of -factor values alternates signs. For the growing square arrangement with totals 1,5,14,... each new step adds n^2, so S(1)=1 and S(n)=S(n-1)+n^2; S(4)=30. For maximal planar pieces from n straight cuts, R(n)=1+n(n+1)/2.

Activity 6.1: Reading Representations: math source context — For each sequence shown, find either the growth factor or rate of change. Be prepared to explain your reasoning. 5, 15, 25, 35, 45, . . . Starting at 10, each new term is \(\frac52\) less than the previous term. \(g(1)=\text-5, g(n)=g(n-1)\boldcdot \text-2\) for \(n\ge2\). Work the source task, document quantities and justify the rule. Teacher checks any diagram, model or partner discussion.

Activity 6.2: Matching Recursive Definitions: math source context — Take turns with your partner to match a sequence with a recursive definition. It may help to first figure out if the sequence is arithmetic or geometric. For each match that you find, explain to your partner how you know it’s a match. For each match that your partner finds, listen carefully to their explanation. If. Work the source task, document quantities and justify the rule. Teacher checks any diagram, model or partner discussion.

Activity 6.3: Squares of Squares: math source context — Here is a pattern where the number of small squares increases with each new step. Write a recursive definition for the total number of small squares \(S(n)\) in Step \(n\). Sketch a graph of \(S\) that shows Steps 1 to 7. Is this sequence geometric, arithmetic, or neither? Be prepared to explain how you know. Start. Work the source task, document quantities and justify the rule. Teacher checks any diagram, model or partner discussion.

First-party independent cool-down: A block pattern has S(1)=1 and adds n squared small squares at step n. Find S(2), S(3) and S(4), write its recursive definition and state if arithmetic, geometric or neither. Answer key: S(2)=5,S(3)=14,S(4)=30; S(n)=S(n-1)+n^2 for n>=2; neither.

KeyConcepts.Title: Four representations
KeyConcepts.Definition: One indexed sequence can appear as numbers, table, graph and recurrence.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Keep index and start conditions consistent.

KeyConcepts.Title: Sign-changing geometric sequence
KeyConcepts.Definition: Negative ratio reverses the sign every step.

KeyConcepts.Title: Sum of squares pattern
KeyConcepts.Definition: A new n-by-n block contributes n squared cells.

WorkedExamples.Title: Square growth
WorkedExamples.Question: A pattern totals 1,5,14 squares at steps 1,2,3. What is step 4?
Steps: The added counts are 1,4,9 at the first three steps.

WorkedExamples.Title: Maximum pieces of a circle
WorkedExamples.Question: Starting with one region, how many at most after four straight cuts?
WorkedExamples.Method: Each new line can cross all previous lines at distinct points.
WorkedExamples.Check: A drawing must actually exhibit the maximal intersections.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating a sequence rule as context-free.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: It can alter the index, initial term, units or learning target.
CommonMistakes.Correction: State the beginning term, domain and original lesson model.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Using a fixed common difference when the sequence is not arithmetic.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Differing consecutive differences invalidate the arithmetic formula.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Calculate two or more differences or ratios before selecting a rule.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Auto-grading graphs, card exchanges or manipulative proof from a number alone.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Numeric equality does not establish a correct diagram or explanation.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use a teacher rubric for visual and reasoning evidence.
